solutions.latex:
By the chain rule:

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}f\left(e^x\right)=e^x f'\left(e^x\right)$$

Since $e^x>0$, this is zero only when $f'\left(e^x\right)=0$, that is, when $e^x$ equals the $x$-coordinate of a stationary point of $f$.

$e^x$ takes only positive values. Of the three stationary points of $f$, two have positive $x$-coordinates (near $x=1$ and $x=2$) and one has a negative $x$-coordinate, so $y=f\left(e^x\right)$ has 2 stationary points.

$$f(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{e^x}$$

Using the quotient rule:

$$\begin{aligned} x=0, &\quad 2-x=0 \\ x=0, &\quad x=2 \\ y=0, &\quad y=\dfrac{4}{e^2}=0.541\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{Minimum at } (0,0) \text{ and maximum at } \left(2,\dfrac{4}{e^2}\right)$$

solutions.latex:
The gradients of $y=e\ln x$ and $y=ax^2+c$ at point of intersection are both equal to 1.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(e\ln x) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{e}{x} &= 1 \\ x &= e \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore\ y=e$, so $y=ax^2+c$ has gradient of 1 at point $(e,e)$.

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[ax^2+c\right]=2ax$$

$$\begin{aligned} 2ax &= 1 \quad\text{at } x=e \\ 2a\cdot e &= 1 \\ a &= \dfrac{1}{2e} \end{aligned}$$

and $y=ax^2+c=e$ at $x=e$:

$$\begin{aligned} e &= \dfrac{1}{2e}\cdot e^2+c \\ e &= \dfrac{e}{2}+c \\ c &= \dfrac{e}{2} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{1}{2e},\ c=\dfrac{e}{2}$$

So $2\pi r+3x=100$

That is $r=\dfrac{100-3x}{2\pi}$

$$\begin{aligned} A(x) &= \text{Area of circle}+\text{area of equilateral triangle} \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 60^\circ \\ &= \pi r^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}x^2 \\ &= \pi\left(\dfrac{100-3x}{2\pi}\right)^2+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}x^2 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\sqrt{3}\,x^2+\dfrac{(100-3x)^2}{\pi}\right) \end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: Provides correct solution; 1: Finds an expression for $r$ in terms of $x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$A(x)$ is a quadratic with positive coefficient of $x^2$ so $A$ has a minimum stationary point.

The maximum will therefore occur on an endpoint of the domain.

When $x=0$:

$$r=\dfrac{50}{\pi} \qquad \text{Area}=\pi r^2=\dfrac{50^2}{\pi}\approx 796$$

When $r=0$:

$$x=33\dfrac{1}{3} \qquad \text{Area}=\dfrac{1}{2}x^2\sin 60^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\times 33.333^2\approx 481$$

\exfigure{1630_q26_s1}

$\therefore$ The maximum value of $A(x)$ occurs when all wire is used for the circle.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: Provides correct solution; 2: Finds the value of $A$ at an endpoint, or equivalent merit; 1: Identifies that the quadratic will have a minimum turning point, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Two applications: $n=2$ strips of width $\dfrac{2-0}{2}=1$, so $x_0=0$, $x_1=1$, $x_2=2$ with $f(0)=1$, $f(1)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $f(2)=\dfrac{1}{4}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac{b-a}{2n}\Big\{f(a)+f(b)+2\left[f(x_1)\right]\Big\} \\ &= \dfrac{2-0}{2\times 2}\left\{1+\dfrac{1}{4}+2\times\dfrac{1}{2}\right\} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1+\dfrac{1}{4}+1\right) \\ &= \dfrac{9}{8} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: Provides correct solution; 1: Attempts to use trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx=\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}+C$:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^x dx &= \left[\dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^x}{\ln\frac{1}{2}}\right]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2}{\ln\frac{1}{2}}-\dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^0}{\ln\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{-\frac{3}{4}}{-\ln 2} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4\ln 2} \end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: Provides correct solution; 1: Provides the correct antiderivative of $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The function is concave up, so the exact value is less than the trapezoidal approximation:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{4\ln 2} &< \dfrac{9}{8} \\ 24 &< 36\ln 2 \\ 2 &< 3\ln 2 \\ 2 &< \ln 8 \\ e^2 &< 8 \\ e &< \sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ e<2\sqrt{2}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: Provides correct solution; 1: Provides correct initial inequality, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Area of shaded segment $=$ area of sector $-$ area of triangle, and the segment is $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of the paddock:

$$\text{area of sector}-\text{area of triangle}=\dfrac{1}{4}\times\text{area of circle}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}\times 10^2\theta-\dfrac{1}{2}\times 10^2\sin\theta &= \dfrac{10^2\pi}{4} \\ 50\theta-50\sin\theta &= 25\pi \\ 50(\theta-\sin\theta) &= 25\pi \\ \theta-\sin\theta &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ \theta &= \sin\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: Provides correct solution; 1: Provides a correct expression relating the areas in the diagram, or equivalent merit

In $\triangle TYO$, right-angled at $O$:

$$\begin{aligned} \tan 60^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{OY} \\ \therefore\ OY &= \dfrac{h}{\tan 60^\circ} \\ &= \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$

The exact value $\tan 60^\circ=\sqrt{3}$ comes from the $30^\circ$–$60^\circ$–$90^\circ$ triangle:

solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: Provides correct solution

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle TFO$, $\angle TFO=45^\circ$, $\angle TOF=90^\circ$

$\therefore\ \angle OTF=45^\circ$

$\therefore\ \triangle TFO$ is isosceles and $OF=h$

In $\triangle FOY$, $\angle OYF=45^\circ$ ($F$ is south-west of $Y$ and $O$ is due west of $Y$). By the cosine rule:

$$\begin{aligned} h^2 &= \left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+4^2-2\times 4\times\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\cos 45^\circ \\ h^2 &= \dfrac{h^2}{3}+16-\dfrac{8h}{\sqrt{6}} \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{2h^2}{3}+\dfrac{8h}{\sqrt{6}}-16=0$$

$$\begin{aligned} h &= \dfrac{-\frac{8}{\sqrt{6}}\pm\sqrt{\frac{64}{6}+4\times\frac{2}{3}\times 16}}{\frac{4}{3}} \\ &= 3.03 \quad\text{since } h>0 \end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: Provides correct solution; 2: Finds a quadratic expression in $h$, or equivalent merit; 1: Attempts to use the cosine rule to find a value for $h$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1630_q29_s2}

In $\triangle FOY$, let $\theta=\angle OFY$. By the sine rule:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\frac{h}{\sqrt{3}}} &= \dfrac{\sin 45^\circ}{h} \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{3}} \\ \theta &= 24^\circ\ldots \\ &\approx 24^\circ \end{aligned}$$

$Y$ is on a bearing of $045^\circ$ from $F$, and $O$ is $\theta$ further anticlockwise:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 45^\circ-24^\circ \\ &\approx 021^\circ \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Translating right by $k$ and up by $k$: replace $x$ with $x-k$ and $y$ with $y-k$.

$$\begin{aligned} y-k &= (x-k-1)(x-k-5) \\ 11-k &= (6-k-1)(6-k-5) \\ 11-k &= (5-k)(1-k) \\ 11-k &= 5-6k+k^2 \\ k^2-5k-6 &= 0 \\ (k-6)(k+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So, $k=6$ since $k$ is positive
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: Provides correct solution; 2: Obtains a quadratic in $k$, or equivalent merit; 1: Substitutes $x-k$ and $y-k$ into equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\cos x=\dfrac{1}{2}$$

$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{3},\ \ldots$$

\exfigure{1630_q31_s1}

$y=\cos px$ is a dilation horizontally by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{p}$, so its solutions are these values multiplied by $\dfrac{1}{p}$.

Lowest value of $p$ to get 2 solutions (second solution at $x=2\pi$):

\exfigure{1630_q31_s2}

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{p} &= 2\pi \\ p &= \dfrac{5\pi}{3\times 2\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$

Highest value of $p$ to get 2 solutions (at this value a third solution appears at $x=2\pi$, so it is excluded):

\exfigure{1630_q31_s3}

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{7\pi}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{p} &= 2\pi \\ p &= \dfrac{7\pi}{3\times 2\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{7}{6} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \dfrac{5}{6}\le p<\dfrac{7}{6}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: Provides correct solution; 2: Finds $p=\dfrac{5}{6}$ or $p=\dfrac{7}{6}$, or equivalent merit; 1: Finds $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$, or equivalent merit
